text: You're given the roots of two binary trees, p and q. Return true if they are the same — same structure and same values at every position.

Thanks. Before I dive in, I'd like to clarify a few things. Just to make sure I'm understanding this correctly — same means both things at once: the shape has to match and the values have to match. So one with a left child two, and one with a right child two, are different, even though both have a one and a two. Is that right?

Good. Then I walk both trees in lockstep and compare the two nodes I'm standing on. There are exactly three situations. Both are null — that matches. Exactly one is null — the shapes differ, so no. Both are real — compare values, then recurse into both sides. And two empty trees are the same, so an all-null input is true. Are there any constraints on the input size?
Up to a hundred nodes in each tree. Either can be empty.

Let me run through the example. Take p as one, two, one and q as one, one, two. Both roots are one, so far so good. Then p's left is two and q's left is one, so the answer is false. Same shape, same values, but in different places — a value check at the root alone is not enough.

Hmm, let me think about this for a sec. A naive approach would be to serialize each tree to a string, with markers for the null slots, then compare the strings. That works, but it builds two full strings before it can find a difference that might be at the very first node. This problem reminds me of a parallel depth-first search — the same walk as a normal traversal, just with two pointers moving together. It fits because same tree is defined recursively: the roots match and both subtree pairs match. And it can stop the instant it finds a mismatch.

Here's the plan. One: if at least one pointer is null, return whether p equals q. Two: otherwise, compare the two values. Three: recurse left with left and right with right, all joined by and. One thing worth flagging — that first line looks like a trick. Inside it, at least one pointer is null, so p equals q can only be true if both are null. Two nulls, they match; one null, they don't. Both cases, one line. The two-line version — both null return true, then either null return false — says the same thing more plainly, but I want to be able to justify the one-liner, not just recite it. Does this approach sound good, or would you rather I think of another way?

Alright, let me code this up. The guard handles the null cases, then one return chains the value check and the two recursive calls with and. One thing worth flagging — the guard has to come first, and not only to avoid a crash on p's value. It is what makes p equals q mean both null. That comparison is on pointers, not on trees. If I dropped the guard and compared pointers for every pair, two separate trees with the same content would come out false, because they never share an address.

Let's dry-run the code with an example. p is one, two, one, q is one, one, two, expecting false. The row that matters is the root's left: two against one, so the and short-circuits — neither child pair of that node is visited, and false travels straight back up. Two calls in total; identical trees would have taken seven. Let's also test with corner cases. Both empty: the guard fires and two nulls are equal, so true. One empty: the guard fires, false. Two single nodes with the same value: both child pairs are null pairs, so true. One, two against one, null, two: on the left, a node meets a null, so false.

The time complexity is O of the smaller tree's size — the recursion can't go further than the smaller tree, because the guard stops each branch when one side runs out. The space complexity is O of the smaller height, for the call stack. In the worst-case scenario the answer is true, since nothing short-circuits: two identical chains of a hundred nodes take two hundred one calls, while trees that differ at the root take one. Oh, one more thing — a testing point. If a test harness passes the same object as both p and q, a broken pointer-comparison version passes every equal test, for the wrong reason. An equal pair must be two separate copies with the same content.

Nicely done. Three things stood out. You explained why p equals q is correct only because the guard guarantees one side is null, and what breaks without that guard. You worked out that short-circuiting makes true the expensive case here. And you tied it back to test design — a harness reusing the same object would hide the bug entirely. Good work.
